findings.text: The first sentence tells a newcomer what Athena is and what sets it apart: one model does the work, a different one checks it, and costs are recorded. This is the clearest part of the page.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: Someone who opens Athena's home URL finds a page about a different project, firstmate. Athena gets three lede paragraphs, and everything after them is the firstmate study, so a reader who came to learn about Athena gets little more about it.
This is the only reason the page gives for why Athena matters. It says what the study demonstrates, but not what problem Athena solves for the reader or why to pick it over doing the work by hand.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: The page links to a next step early, which helps a reader who wants to act before reading the whole study.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader already has a checkout. It gives no clone command and no prerequisites (for example a Rust toolchain or AI model access), so a newcomer could get stuck between the link and `athena ask`.
findings.source: Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh

findings.text: A short, concrete first command is a good on-ramp. But the page doesn't say what the reader will see or where the result ends up.
findings.source: Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog"

findings.text: The study defines its terms before using them and follows one piece of work from start to finish. A newcomer to firstmate can follow the main flow without reading the source.
Being honest about a term it cannot define builds trust. But it leaves a key condition of the yolo merge rule unexplained for the reader.
findings.source: <dt>in scope</dt><dd>... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it.

findings.text: The transition cards are packed with special cases and jargon (harness, pin, endpoint, secondmate). A newcomer is likely to skim or give up here.
findings.source: Heading "Transitions", card t8: "A ship or scout keeps its recorded harness and needs a note; a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead."

findings.text: The "Limits of this study" section and the "About this page" section ("the name of the folder under studies/") talk about Athena's internal process and files. That means little to a first-time reader.
findings.source: f3 ... A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths: teardown reopening a backlog item (t9, c23 to c25), ...
